abstract: Precise translation initiation is essential for efficient production of proteins; missing or mis-selecting the canonical start site can have detrimental consequences. Past research identified several initiation factors governing start codon selection accuracy in yeast, but the increasing complexity of higher eukaryotes have limited similar research in mammalian cells. We present an in cellulo study of knock-in mutants of the eIF3c subunit of the multitasking eIF3 complex that disrupt eIF3's interaction with eIF5, thereby preventing functional binding of eIF5 to pre-initiation complexes. This selectively relaxes start site selection stringency and reduces initiation sensitivity, leading to altered translation efficiency for nearly 600 proteins. Proteins with N-terminal targeting signals were among those especially affected, resulting in impaired mitochondrial function. These findings establish the first direct causal link between an initiation factor, stringent start site recognition, and impaired mitochondrial respiration and glycolytic activity, implicating the eIF3-eIF5 interaction as a key regulator of energy homeostasis.
